messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 61
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Non-profit Worker
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 42

He is a 61-year-old South Asian man who has spent much of his life working in the nonprofit world, moving between community meetings, donor calls, and difficult conversations with families in crisis. He has always seen himself as someone who stays useful when others are overwhelmed. That sense of purpose is part of what makes the accident so hard to absorb. Before the collision, he is the kind of man who leaves early, keeps spare reading glasses in the glove compartment, and prides himself on being reliable to his wife and colleagues. He rarely complains about pain and has long been the one other people lean on.

The collision happens on an ordinary afternoon, when he is driving home after a work meeting. He remembers the weather, the light, the ordinary rhythm of traffic. Then, in an instant, everything changes. Another vehicle comes toward him in a way he cannot avoid. The impact is violent and disorienting. He recalls the sound more than the sight at first: metal crumpling, glass breaking, his own breath catching in his throat. For a few seconds he believes he may die there, trapped and unable to move. What stays with him most is not only the fear but the helplessness. He is used to being the one who can solve problems, yet in that moment he cannot do anything except wait and try to stay conscious.

In the weeks after, he tells people he is “fine,” but he is not fine in the way they mean. He returns home physically intact enough to be released from the hospital, yet his body does not settle back into its old rhythm. He startles at sudden sounds, especially the sharp slap of a car door or the squeal of brakes outside his window. He begins scanning intersections before he even reaches them, his shoulders tightening as he approaches each stoplight. At first he insists on driving again because he does not want fear to shrink his world, but he finds himself gripping the steering wheel so tightly that his hands ache. Sometimes he has to pull over and sit with his head lowered, waiting for the shaking to pass.

Sleep becomes unreliable. He lies awake replaying the moment of impact, trying to understand how quickly everything became dangerous. When he does fall asleep, he wakes abruptly with his heart pounding, convinced for a few seconds that he is back in the car. He grows tired during the day and less patient with small frustrations. At work, where he once moved easily from one responsibility to the next, he now loses concentration. He reads the same email several times without taking it in. In meetings, he is present in body but not always in the room. He notices that he is more irritable, especially when people move too quickly around him or speak over one another. The chaos of busy offices, which once felt manageable, now makes him feel cornered.

He also notices himself pulling away from things that used to matter. He has always valued family meals and community gatherings, but now he sometimes finds excuses to stay home. His wife sees how much effort it takes for him to keep up appearances. He does not want to alarm her, so he minimizes his distress, yet she can see that he is quieter and more watchful. He feels ashamed of how easily he is shaken. As a man who has built a life around steadiness and service, he struggles with the idea that one accident has changed him so much. There are moments when he feels angry at his own body for not “moving on” and angry at the world for how fragile ordinary life can be.

Over time, he becomes increasingly aware that the accident is not only an event in the past but something that continues to live inside him. Certain intersections bring a surge of dread. The smell of burned rubber, the sound of tires on wet pavement, and the sight of damaged cars can make his chest tighten before he has time to think. He tries to push these reactions aside, but they return in flashes of image and sensation, as though his mind is still trying to catch up with what happened. Even now, months later, he remains someone who is functioning on the outside while internally bracing against reminders that he has not fully escaped the collision.
